description: Predictive vs Agile vs hybrid — and how to pick one.

screens.body:
Software development is writing the code. Software engineering is the discipline wrapped around it: planning, requirements, design, testing, and managing the people doing the work — so the code actually ships and keeps working.

In a project context, the difference matters because code is only one slice of the work. A brilliant coder with no plan still ships late.

options: Planning, process, and teamwork around the code
check.question: Software engineering adds…

screens.heading: Development vs engineering
screens.keyPoint: Engineering is the discipline that gets code shipped.

screens.body:
Predictive models (like waterfall) plan everything up front: requirements, then design, then code, then test — each phase finishing before the next starts. You predict the whole journey before taking step one.

This shines when requirements are stable and the cost of change is brutal: think medical devices, construction software, fixed-price contracts. It suffers when the client says 'actually…' in month four.

options: Stable requirements, high cost of change
check.question: Predictive fits best with…

screens.heading: Predictive: plan it all first
screens.keyPoint: Waterfall works when change is expensive and scope is stable.

screens.body:
Agile flips it: build in short loops (iterations or sprints), show working software early, and let feedback reshape the plan. Requirements evolve because the client learns what they want by seeing it.

The Agile Manifesto values working software, customer collaboration, and responding to change over rigid plans. Agile isn't 'no planning' — it's planning continuously, in small slices.

options: Short loops with feedback reshaping the plan
check.question: Agile means…

screens.heading: Agile: build in small loops
screens.keyPoint: Working software early, feedback often, plans adapt.

screens.body:
Real teams rarely live at the extremes. Hybrid takes the skeleton from predictive — a rough plan, milestones, a budget — and runs the day-to-day work in agile loops.

Example: the release date and major features are fixed (predictive shell), but each feature is designed and built in two-week sprints with client demos (agile core). Match the mix to your constraints.

options: Predictive shell with agile day-to-day work
Half the team agile, half waterfall
check.question: A hybrid approach mixes…

screens.heading: Hybrid: mix to fit

screens.body:
Ask four questions. How clear are the requirements? (Fuzzy → agile.) How often can the client give feedback? (Rarely → predictive.) How big is the team? (Huge → more structure.) What's the cost of a mistake? (Lives or millions → predictive.)

There's no moral ranking — only fit. Picking agile for a pacemaker and waterfall for a social app are both mistakes.

options: How clear requirements are and how often feedback comes
check.question: To choose a model, first ask…

screens.heading: Choosing a model
screens.keyPoint: Fit the model to the project's uncertainty.

screens.body:
Scrum is the most common agile framework. Three roles: the product owner (decides WHAT to build), the scrum master (protects the process), and the developers (build it).

Work runs in sprints (1–4 weeks) with four rituals: sprint planning, daily standups, a sprint review demo, and a retrospective on how to improve. The backlog — a prioritized to-do list — feeds every sprint.

options: The person who writes all the code
The person who prioritizes what gets built
The person who funds the project
check.question: The product owner is…

screens.heading: Scrum in one screen
screens.keyPoint: Roles, sprints, backlog, and four rituals.

screens.body:
Process needs tooling. Kanban boards (Trello, Jira) make work visible. Repos with pull requests make code review the norm. Shared docs and chat keep decisions written down instead of lost in hallway talk.

CASE tools — computer-aided software engineering — are tools that help you build software: diagram editors, project trackers, test runners. The tool doesn't replace the process, but a good one makes the process painless.
screens.heading: Tools that hold it together
screens.keyPoint: Tools make process visible and painless.

screens.body: The Agile Manifesto — agilemanifesto.org. The Scrum Guide — scrum.org. (Both are short reads and worth your time.)
screens.heading: Go deeper
screens.keyPoint: Read the Manifesto and the Scrum Guide.
